title: ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended And Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
mutable_substrate: Task-scoped executable program code inside EVOLVE-BLOCK markers. The demonstrations mutate a Python circle-packing optimizer, a Python AIME multi-agent scaffold, C++ ALE-Bench heuristic solvers, and a PyTorch mixture-of-experts load-balancing loss; ShinkaEvolve's own search engine and evaluator remain fixed.

optimization_operator.parent_selection: Hierarchical island selection followed by power-law rank sampling or a weighted sampler whose fitness sigmoid is multiplied by 1/(1+offspring_count).
proposal_mutations: Crossover with an additional archive program
optimization_operator.proposal_allocation: A UCB1-style multi-armed bandit adapts LLM sampling using exponentially amplified positive fitness improvement over the stronger of the parent and initial-program baselines.
optimization_operator.novelty_filter: Mutable-code embeddings are compared within the island; proposals above cosine similarity 0.95 can be rejected or sent to an LLM novelty judge before expensive execution.
optimization_operator.search_memory: Periodic meta-agent summaries turn recent evaluations into global insights and up to five implementation recommendations appended to later mutation prompts.

feedback_selection: A task-specific evaluator returns scalar fitness, public metrics, and textual feedback. Scalar fitness drives parent sampling and archive survival, while metrics and feedback condition later LLM mutations. Invalid patches or edits to immutable code are resampled with parsing feedback. The framework calls this multi-objective assessment, but the paper does not define a multi-objective environmental-selection rule over the public metrics.

archive_memory.archive: Fixed-size evaluated-program archive with fitness, metadata, public metrics, and text feedback.
archive_memory.population_structure: Two to four island subpopulations seeded from the same initial program; non-champion members may migrate, while each island's best program is protected from migration.
archive_memory.inspiration_context: A primary parent is augmented with random archive programs and top-performing inspiration programs.
archive_memory.long_term_summary: A periodically regenerated meta-scratchpad stores individual summaries, successful and ineffective patterns, implementation insights, and actionable recommendations.
archive_memory.capacity: Reported archive sizes are 40 for circle packing, 40 for AIME, 50 for ALE-Bench, and 20 for MoE-loss discovery.

validation_strategy: Circle packing uses an OpenEvolve verifier with 1e-6 slack, then AlphaEvolve's exact verifier after shrinking each radius by 1e-8; a separate evolution also uses the exact verifier throughout.
AIME evaluates each candidate three times on all 30 AIME 2024 problems, then tests the selected scaffold on AIME 2023 and 2025 and transfers it to gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1, and o4-mini.
ALE-Bench uses public test scores for evolution and private AtCoder test scores for final top-1 and diagnostic top-5 comparisons.

MoE loss discovery evolves on a 556M-parameter model trained for 2.10B tokens, then validates on a 2.7B-parameter model trained for 29.36B tokens at three auxiliary-loss coefficients and on seven downstream benchmarks.
Component ablations compare parent sampling, single versus ensemble versus bandit model allocation, and no versus embedding versus embedding-plus-LLM novelty rejection on circle packing.
adaptation_mode: Task-time, offline evolutionary optimization of a bounded program over a sequence of evaluator calls. Archives and bandit statistics update continually during a run, and an asynchronous mode is discussed, but the reported artifacts are selected after search rather than self-modifying during production deployment.

benchmarks.name: 26-circle packing in a unit square
benchmarks.budget: 150 evaluated proposals in the main relaxed-verifier run; roughly 500 in the separate exact-verifier run
benchmarks.metric: sum of circle radii under non-overlap and containment constraints

benchmarks.name: AIME 2024 with transfer to AIME 2023/2025
benchmarks.budget: 75 generations, three candidate evaluations, 30 problems, at most 10 LLM calls per problem

benchmarks.name: ALE-Bench LITE
benchmarks.budget: 10 tasks and 50 generations per initialized solver
benchmarks.metric: public-test evolutionary fitness and private-test contest score

benchmarks.name: FineWeb MoE pretraining plus seven reasoning benchmarks
benchmarks.budget: small 556M/2.10B-token evolution proxy and large 2.7B/29.36B-token validation
benchmarks.metric: cross-entropy, load imbalance, perplexity, missrouting, and mean accuracy over CommonSenseQA, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande, and ARC

principal_results: The relaxed circle-packing run finds sum of radii 2.635983099011548 within 150 proposals; reducing every radius by 1e-8 gives exact-verifier score 2.6359828390115476. A separate exact-verifier evolution reaches 2.63597770931127 in roughly 500 proposals.
The main circle-packing proposal-API cost curve ends near $12; the longer exact-verifier curve ends near $43. Evaluator compute is not included.

The evolved seven-call AIME scaffold scores 34.4% on AIME 2024 versus 24.4% for the base agent, transfers at 23.0% on 2023 and 20.0% on 2025, and reaches 65.6%, 65.6%, and 94.4% with gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1, and o4-mini.
On AIME 2025, Majority@5 scores 25.6% and exceeds the ShinkaEvolve scaffold's 20.0%, although both improve over the 11.1% base.
ALE-Bench public top-1 selection improves the private mean from 1879.3 to 1923.5, about 2.35%; ahc039 improves from score 2880 and hypothetical fifth place to 3140 and hypothetical second place.
The evolved MoE loss improves seven-benchmark mean accuracy from 0.3670/0.3620/0.3567 to 0.3702/0.3683/0.3658 at lambda 0.001/0.01/0.1 and slightly lowers perplexity at all three settings.

Circle-packing ablations finish near 2.63/2.57/2.45 for weighted sampling/hill climbing/Best-of-N, 2.63/2.61/2.43 for bandit ensemble/fixed ensemble/single LLM, and 2.63/2.56/2.47 for embedding-plus-LLM/embedding-only/no novelty rejection.
limitations: The current system is not truly open-ended: humans define the task, objective, initial program, evaluator, mutable region, and search configuration; self-generated objectives are future work.
Evaluation counts are not comparable across domains, and sample-efficient proposal search can still be extremely expensive when each candidate requires billions of pretraining tokens.
Most evolutionary results lack independent search repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, and statistical tests; AIME repeats candidate evaluation but not the full search.
AIME searches on all 30 AIME 2024 problems without an internal held-out set, and 2025 transfer underperforms Majority@5.
ALE solutions often remain close to ALE-Agent initialization, suggesting seed-basin overfitting; public/private selection mitigates but does not eliminate it.
Novelty uses code embeddings and an LLM judge rather than behavioral diversity, and no calibration, rejection-rate, false-positive, latency, or net-cost analysis is reported.
Scratchpad accuracy, staleness, prompt growth, contradiction handling, and forgetting are not measured.
The paper claims weighted selection works across all tasks, but displays the ablation only on circle packing and uses significance language without statistical tests.
MoE evolution is described as 30 iterations in prose but 20 generations in the hyperparameter table; ALE top-5 private mean is 1927.0 in prose and 1927.9 in Figure 7.

Figure 8's panel order is reversed in prose, the MoE architecture table repeats the label Model parameters for total and active values, and a missrouting fraction plot has values above one without explanation.
The released MoE loss code uses threshold 0.01*(64/N_E)=0.64/N_E, whereas the manuscript equation gives 0.064/N_E, a factor-of-ten implementation/equation discrepancy.
The code is open source but many experiments depend on proprietary, changing model APIs and prices.
safety_controls: EVOLVE-BLOCK markers constrain the writable code region, and proposed patches that alter immutable code are rejected.
Malformed patches can be resampled with parsing feedback before evaluator execution.
The evaluation API supports optional validation, multi-run aggregation, and public metrics visible to evolution alongside private metrics hidden for audit.
Circle packing receives a separate exact-verifier check, and ALE-Bench uses private tests after public-fitness search.

No mandatory sandbox, filesystem or network permission model, secret isolation, dependency policy, malicious-code screening, execution quota, human approval gate, audit log, or rollback control is specified for generated programs.

explicit_predecessors.name: AlphaEvolve
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit methodological predecessor and primary circle-packing comparison.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper names AlphaEvolve as one of the closest systems, follows its SEARCH/REPLACE diff-edit and EVOLVE-BLOCK conventions, uses its exact circle verifier, and claims a higher circle-packing score with fewer than 150 proposals.

explicit_predecessors.name: Darwin Gödel Machine
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit inspiration for performance-and-novelty weighted parent selection.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The parent-sampling section states that weighted sampling is inspired by Zhang et al. 2025 and uses both fitness and number of offspring; that citation is Darwin Gödel Machine.

explicit_predecessors.name: FunSearch
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit foundation for island-model program evolution and mathematical program discovery.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The archive section follows Romera-Paredes et al. 2024 for independent island subpopulations, migration, and protection of island elites.

explicit_predecessors.name: OpenEvolve
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit open-source interface and experimental predecessor.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: OpenEvolve is named among the closest systems; ShinkaEvolve roughly adopts its high-level Python API and uses its circle-packing verifier and baseline implementation.

explicit_predecessors.name: LLM4AD
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit related program-evolution system and circle-packing baseline.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: LLM4AD is listed among the closest related systems and appears in the circle-packing score comparison.

explicit_predecessors.name: Reflexion
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit mechanism reused for invalid-patch feedback and resampling.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: After checking immutable code, ShinkaEvolve provides parsing feedback and resamples invalid proposals using the Reflexion pattern.

explicit_predecessors.name: UCB1
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit algorithmic basis for adaptive proposal-model selection.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The adaptive LLM sampler associates every model with visits and estimated relative-improvement reward and updates model probabilities with a UCB1-based strategy.

explicit_predecessors.name: ALE-Agent
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit task-specific predecessor and initialization source.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Every ALE-Bench search starts from ALE-Agent's best discovered program, and improvements are measured against those seeds on public and private tests.

open_questions: Can search policies, novelty thresholds, archive sizes, migration rates, mutation scopes, and scratchpad intervals adapt automatically without destabilizing search?
How should proposal sample efficiency be compared when evaluator cost ranges from a numerical function to 2.10B-token model pretraining?
Can behavioral novelty, execution traces, or test-output diversity complement code embeddings and reduce false novelty decisions?
What repeated-run variance and statistical significance remain after changing random seeds, model samples, asynchronous scheduling, and archive initialization?
How can meta-scratchpads be verified, bounded, deduplicated, forgotten, and protected from evaluator or proposal-model hallucinations?
Which release discipline prevents generated code from accessing secrets, networks, filesystems, or excessive compute while preserving useful experimentation?
Can held-out evaluator suites and adversarial tests prevent reward hacking of slack, parsing, public tests, or training proxies?
Does the evolved MoE loss transfer to different expert counts, top-K values, routers, data domains, training schedules, and production-scale models?
Which MoE threshold is authoritative: the manuscript's 0.064/N_E or the released code's 0.64/N_E, and were reported runs produced by the latter?
Can asynchronous evolution correct for stale archives and latency-based model bias while retaining throughput gains?
What mechanism would make the system genuinely open-ended by generating useful and safe objectives rather than merely optimizing human-specified ones?
